## Goal, in plain English

Open a normal desktop window. That is it. No real graphics yet.

Tutorial: https://sotrh.github.io/learn-wgpu/beginner/tutorial1-window/

This lives at `examples/ch01_window.rs`.

## What you are learning

- `winit` = the Rust library that creates a window and receives keyboard/mouse/window events.
- `wgpu` = the Rust graphics library we will use later to draw with the GPU.
- `env_logger` = prints useful log messages while the program runs.
- `State` = a struct where we keep app data. For now it mostly holds the window.
- `resize()` = code that runs when the window size changes.
- `render()` = code that will draw a frame later. For this issue, it can be an empty placeholder.

## What to build

1. Add the needed dependencies from Learn Wgpu chapter 1.
2. Make `examples/ch01_window.rs`.
3. Open a native desktop window.
4. Give the window your own title.
5. Start the window at a non-default size, for example `1280x720`.
6. Make closing the window work.
7. Make pressing `Escape` close the program.
8. Make a `State` struct that stores the window, for example `Arc<Window>`.
9. Add empty `resize(w, h)` and `render()` methods so later chapters have a place to grow.
10. Wire `WindowEvent::Resized` and `WindowEvent::RedrawRequested` through `ApplicationHandler`.

## Do not build this yet

Skip all browser / WebAssembly work.

That means you do **not** need:

- `wasm-pack`
- `wasm-bindgen`
- `web-sys`
- `console_log`
- `run_web()`
- any `cfg(target_arch = "wasm32")` code
- any browser build setup

This project is desktop-only for now.

## Done when

- [ ] `cargo run --example ch01_window` opens a window
- [ ] Window has your custom title and a non-default starting size
- [ ] Closing the window exits cleanly
- [ ] Pressing `Escape` exits cleanly
- [ ] There are no warnings about missing `winit` features you should have enabled
- [ ] A `State` struct holds the window and has `resize(w, h)` and `render()` stubs
- [ ] `WindowEvent::Resized` and `WindowEvent::RedrawRequested` are handled through `ApplicationHandler`

## Depends on

Nothing. Start here.

## Time estimate

Local estimate: **2–4 hours** of focused work.

Assumes basic Rust knowledge, no prior graphics experience, and the type-along + small-variation working pattern. This is a local estimate for this issue only; see `README.md` for the global cursus estimate.
issues.title: ch01: Dependencies and the window

## Goal, in plain English

Make the window clear itself to a color every frame.

This is the first tiny GPU step. You are not drawing shapes yet. You are just asking the GPU to fill the window with one color.

Tutorial: https://sotrh.github.io/learn-wgpu/beginner/tutorial2-surface/

This lives at `examples/ch02_surface.rs`.

## What you are learning

- `Surface` = the drawable part of the window. Think: "the place the GPU paints into."
- Adapter = the graphics hardware/backend `wgpu` chooses.
- Device = the main object you use to create GPU resources.
- Queue = the thing you use to send work to the GPU.
- Clear color = the background color used to wipe the frame before drawing.
- Validation error = `wgpu` telling you "the GPU setup is wrong." Treat these as useful warnings, not scary magic.

## What to build

1. Follow Learn Wgpu chapter 2.
2. Create the `wgpu` surface for the window.
3. Request an adapter and device.
4. Configure the surface.
5. Every frame, clear the window to a solid color.
6. Handle window resizing without crashing.
7. Reuse the window setup from chapter 1 if it helps.

## Extra beginner-friendly variation

Make the background color react to the mouse position:

- mouse x position controls red
- mouse y position controls green
- blue stays constant

So moving the mouse should smoothly change the window color.

## Done when

- [ ] `cargo run --example ch02_surface` opens a window with a colored background
- [ ] Resizing the window does not panic or crash
- [ ] Moving the mouse over the window changes the clear color smoothly
- [ ] Closing the window exits cleanly
- [ ] No `wgpu` validation errors appear at startup or during resize

Tip: run with logging, for example:

```bash
RUST_LOG=wgpu_core=warn,wgpu_hal=warn cargo run --example ch02_surface
```

## Depends on

Finish #1 first.

## Time estimate

Local estimate: **4–8 hours** of focused work.

Assumes basic Rust knowledge, no prior graphics experience, and the type-along + small-variation working pattern. This is a local estimate for this issue only; see `README.md` for the global cursus estimate.

issues.body:
## Goal, in plain English

Draw one triangle.

This is the first time you make the GPU run your own shader code.

Tutorial: https://sotrh.github.io/learn-wgpu/beginner/tutorial3-pipeline/

This lives at `examples/ch03_pipeline.rs`.

## What you are learning

- Shader = small program that runs on the GPU.
- WGSL = the shader language used by `wgpu`.
- Vertex shader = decides where triangle points go on the screen.
- Fragment shader = decides what color each pixel should be.
- Render pipeline = the full GPU recipe for drawing something.
- Screen-space x position = the pixel's horizontal position on the screen.

## What to build

1. Follow Learn Wgpu chapter 3.
2. Write a WGSL vertex shader.
3. Write a WGSL fragment shader.
4. Create a render pipeline.
5. Draw a single triangle.

## Extra beginner-friendly variation

Make the triangle use two solid colors:

- left half = color A
- right half = color B

Use the fragment's screen x position to pick the color.

In plain English: if the pixel is on the left side of the triangle, paint it one color. If it is on the right side, paint it another color.

## Done when

- [ ] `cargo run --example ch03_pipeline` shows a triangle
- [ ] The triangle is split vertically into two colors
- [ ] No `wgpu` validation errors appear at startup

## Depends on

Finish #2 first.

## Time estimate

Local estimate: **6–10 hours** of focused work.

Assumes basic Rust knowledge, no prior graphics experience, and the type-along + small-variation working pattern. This is a local estimate for this issue only; see `README.md` for the global cursus estimate.

issues.body:
## Goal, in plain English

Draw a hexagon using vertex and index buffers.

A hexagon is a 6-sided shape. The GPU still draws triangles, so you will build the hexagon out of 6 triangles.

Tutorial: https://sotrh.github.io/learn-wgpu/beginner/tutorial4-buffer/

This lives at `examples/ch04_buffers.rs`.

## What you are learning

- Vertex = one point in a shape. It can store position, color, texture coordinates, etc.
- Vertex buffer = GPU memory that stores vertices.
- Index buffer = GPU memory that says which vertices make each triangle.
- Interpolation = the GPU smoothly blends values, like colors, between vertices.

## What to build

1. Follow Learn Wgpu chapter 4.
2. Move triangle data into a vertex buffer.
3. Add an index buffer.
4. Draw a regular hexagon.
5. Use 7 vertices total:
   - 6 outer points
   - 1 center point
6. Use 18 indices total:
   - 6 triangles
   - 3 indices per triangle
7. Give each vertex a different color so the hexagon has a smooth color gradient.

## Simple mental model

Think of the center vertex as the middle of a pizza. Each triangle is one pizza slice.

## Done when

- [ ] `cargo run --example ch04_buffers` shows a hexagon
- [ ] An index buffer is used
- [ ] The hexagon shows smooth color blending between vertices
- [ ] Vertex count is 7
- [ ] Index count is 18

## Depends on

Finish #3 first.

## Time estimate

Local estimate: **5–8 hours** of focused work.

Assumes basic Rust knowledge, no prior graphics experience, and the type-along + small-variation working pattern. This is a local estimate for this issue only; see `README.md` for the global cursus estimate.
issues.title: ch04: Buffers and Indices

issues.body:
## Goal, in plain English

Put an image on a rectangle.

This teaches textures: images that the GPU can read while drawing.

Tutorial: https://sotrh.github.io/learn-wgpu/beginner/tutorial5-textures/

## Important project rule

Build this in the main shared code path, not as a totally separate throwaway program. Use shared `src/` code where it makes sense.

## What you are learning

- Texture = an image stored on the GPU.
- Sampler = tells the GPU how to read a texture, especially when it is scaled.
- Bind group = the package of GPU resources a shader can use.
- Fragment shader = decides the color of each pixel.
- Texel = one pixel inside a texture image.
- Uniform = a small value sent from CPU code to shader code.
- `vec4<f32>` = four floating-point numbers. For colors this usually means red, green, blue, alpha.

## What to build

1. Follow Learn Wgpu chapter 5.
2. Load an image file.
3. Create a GPU texture from it.
4. Create a sampler.
5. Create a bind group so the shader can access the texture.
6. Draw a textured quad. A quad is just a rectangle made from two triangles.

## Extra beginner-friendly variation

Use your own image instead of the tutorial image.

Also add a `tint: vec4<f32>` uniform and multiply the sampled texture color by it in the fragment shader.

In plain English: draw the image, but push its colors toward another color, like warm orange.

## Done when

- [ ] `cargo run` shows a textured quad
- [ ] The texture is your own image, not the tutorial image
- [ ] The tint visibly changes the image colors
- [ ] There are no bind group layout mismatch validation errors

## Depends on

Finish #4 first.

## Time estimate

Local estimate: **6–10 hours** of focused work.

Assumes basic Rust knowledge, no prior graphics experience, and the type-along + small-variation working pattern. This is a local estimate for this issue only; see `README.md` for the global cursus estimate.

issues.body:
## Goal, in plain English

Add a 3D camera so you can move around a scene.

Tutorial: https://sotrh.github.io/learn-wgpu/beginner/tutorial6-uniforms/

## Important project rule

Build this in the main app using shared `src/` code. Do not make a totally separate implementation.

This is also the first chapter where the code may start feeling repetitive. If shared helper code makes the project easier to understand, extract it. Do not extract just because a file is big.

## What you are learning

- Camera = the virtual eye looking at the scene.
- View matrix = where the camera is and where it points.
- Projection matrix = how 3D space gets squashed onto the 2D screen.
- View-projection matrix = view and projection combined.
- Uniform buffer = GPU memory for small shared values, like the camera matrix.
- Bind group = lets the shader read that uniform buffer.
- WASD controls = keyboard movement, like many PC games.
- Active camera = the camera currently being used to render.

## What to build

1. Follow Learn Wgpu chapter 6.
2. Build a `Camera` with view and projection matrices.
3. Send the camera view-projection matrix to the GPU through a uniform buffer.
4. Bind that uniform buffer during the render pass.
5. Add WASD camera movement.

## Extra beginner-friendly variation

Add a second camera.

- Camera 1 starts in one position.
- Camera 2 starts somewhere else.
- Press a key, for example `C`, to switch which camera is active.
- Each camera remembers its own position when you switch away from it.

## Done when

- [ ] `cargo run` shows the textured quad in 3D space
- [ ] WASD moves the active camera
- [ ] Pressing the toggle key switches between the two cameras
- [ ] Each camera keeps its own position/orientation when inactive
- [ ] The camera view-projection matrix is sent through a uniform buffer and bind group
- [ ] The bind group is bound during the render pass
- [ ] The camera matrix is not sent as vertex attributes or push constants

## Depends on

Finish #5 first.

## Time estimate

Local estimate: **8–12 hours** of focused work.

Assumes basic Rust knowledge, no prior graphics experience, and the type-along + small-variation working pattern. This is a local estimate for this issue only; see `README.md` for the global cursus estimate.
issues.title: ch06: Uniform buffers and a 3D camera

issues.body:
## Goal, in plain English

Draw many copies of the same mesh efficiently.

Instead of telling the GPU "draw this shape" 100 separate times, you tell it once: "draw this shape 100 times, but put each copy in a different place."

Tutorial: https://sotrh.github.io/learn-wgpu/beginner/tutorial7-instancing/

## Important project rule

Build this in the main app using shared `src/` code. Do not make a totally separate implementation.

If you have now copied the same camera/window setup 3 or more times, consider moving shared code into `lib.rs` or helper modules. Only do this if it makes the code easier to understand.

## What you are learning

- Instance = one copy of a mesh.
- Instanced rendering = drawing many copies with one draw call.
- Draw call = one command telling the GPU to draw.
- Transform = position, rotation, and scale for an object.
- Per-instance data = data that is different for each copy.
- `VertexStepMode::Instance` = tells `wgpu`: "advance this buffer once per instance, not once per vertex."
- Rule of three = if you copy similar code 3 times, it may be time to extract a helper.

## What to build

1. Follow Learn Wgpu chapter 7.
2. Use instanced rendering.
3. Draw about 100 copies of one mesh.
4. Put each copy in an outward spiral, like a snail shell.
5. Rotate each copy so it faces along the spiral path.

## Done when

- [ ] `cargo run` shows about 100 instances in a spiral
- [ ] The code uses one draw call for the instances, for example one `draw_indexed`
- [ ] Instances visually follow the spiral direction
- [ ] Per-instance data is in a separate buffer using `VertexStepMode::Instance`
- [ ] Per-instance data is not duplicated into the vertex buffer
- [ ] Per-instance data is not pushed as uniforms one object at a time
- [ ] If you started `lib.rs`, write an `IDEAS.md` note explaining why

## Depends on

Finish #6 first.

## Time estimate

Local estimate: **5–8 hours** of focused work.

Assumes basic Rust knowledge, no prior graphics experience, and the type-along + small-variation working pattern. This is a local estimate for this issue only; see `README.md` for the global cursus estimate.
issues.title: ch07: Instancing

issues.body:
## Goal, in plain English

Make closer objects correctly appear in front of farther objects.

Without a depth buffer, the GPU can draw things in the wrong order. A far object might appear on top of a near object. The depth buffer fixes that.

Tutorial: https://sotrh.github.io/learn-wgpu/beginner/tutorial8-depth/

## Important project rule

Build this in the main app using shared `src/` code. Do not make a totally separate implementation.

## What you are learning

- Depth = how far a pixel is from the camera.
- Depth buffer = a hidden image that stores depth values.
- Depth texture = the GPU texture used for the depth buffer.
- Depth-stencil state = pipeline settings that turn depth testing on.
- Occlude = hide behind something closer.
- Grayscale = black/white image. Here it helps you see the depth buffer.

## What to build

1. Follow Learn Wgpu chapter 8.
2. Create a depth texture.
3. Add depth-stencil state to the render pipeline.
4. Use the depth texture while rendering.
5. Recreate the depth texture whenever the window is resized.

## Extra beginner-friendly variation

Add a key toggle, for example `D`.

While the key is held, show the depth buffer on the screen as grayscale instead of the normal colors.

Pick one rule and stay consistent:

- closer = brighter, farther = darker
- or closer = darker, farther = brighter

## Done when

- [ ] `cargo run` shows overlapping 3D geometry in the correct front/back order
- [ ] Holding the toggle key shows the depth buffer as grayscale
- [ ] The depth view clearly shows depth changes, not a flat white/black screen
- [ ] The depth texture is recreated on window resize

## Depends on

Finish #7 first.

## Time estimate

Local estimate: **4–7 hours** of focused work.

Assumes basic Rust knowledge, no prior graphics experience, and the type-along + small-variation working pattern. This is a local estimate for this issue only; see `README.md` for the global cursus estimate.
issues.title: ch08: The Depth Buffer

## Goal, in plain English

Load real 3D model files and draw them.

Tutorial: https://sotrh.github.io/learn-wgpu/beginner/tutorial9-models/

## Important project rule

Build this in the main app using shared `src/` code. Do not make a totally separate implementation.

## What you are learning

- `.obj` = a common 3D model file format.
- `tobj` = a Rust crate that loads `.obj` files.
- Mesh = the shape data for a model.
- Material = settings for how the model should look, often including textures.
- Texture = image data used on the model surface.
- Per-mesh draw = drawing each mesh piece with the right material.
- DCC tool = a 3D art program, like Blender.
- `.gitignore` = tells Git not to track certain files.

## What to build

1. Follow Learn Wgpu chapter 9.
2. Load `.obj` models using `tobj`.
3. Load their materials and textures.
4. Draw the meshes with the right materials.
5. Make the camera controls good enough to inspect the models.

## Extra beginner-friendly variation

Load two different `.obj` models side by side.

- One can be the tutorial cube.
- The other can be a free model from the internet or a simple model you make in Blender.
- Put them apart on the x-axis so you can clearly see both.

If a model file is large, do not commit it. Add it to `.gitignore` and leave a code comment or README note explaining where to get it.

## Done when

- [ ] `cargo run` shows two different models at the same time
- [ ] Each model uses its own material/texture
- [ ] Camera controls let you fly around and inspect both models
- [ ] Large `.obj` files are not committed
- [ ] Large model files are documented so you can download/find them again

## Depends on

Finish #8 first.

## Time estimate

Local estimate: **6–10 hours** of focused work.

Assumes basic Rust knowledge, no prior graphics experience, and the type-along + small-variation working pattern. This is a local estimate for this issue only; see `README.md` for the global cursus estimate.
issues.title: ch09: Model Loading

issues.body:
## Goal, in plain English

Add lighting so 3D objects look shaded instead of flat.

Tutorial: https://sotrh.github.io/learn-wgpu/intermediate/tutorial10-lighting/

## Important project rule

Build this in the main app using shared `src/` code. Do not make a totally separate implementation.

## What you are learning

- Light source = something that brightens the scene.
- Point light = light that shines from one position in all directions.
- Directional light = light from one direction, like sunlight.
- Fragment shader = decides each pixel's color.
- Blinn-Phong = a classic lighting formula.
- Ambient = base light so shadows are not pure black.
- Diffuse = matte light based on surface direction.
- Specular = shiny highlight.
- Render pipeline = GPU recipe for drawing one kind of thing.
- Delta time = seconds since last frame. Use this so motion speed does not depend on FPS.
- Judder = ugly uneven motion.

## What to build

1. Follow Learn Wgpu chapter 10.
2. Add a light.
3. Write lighting math in the fragment shader.
4. Render a small visible marker for the light, like a tiny cube or sphere.
5. Use a separate render pipeline for the light marker.

## Extra beginner-friendly variation

Animate the light so it slowly orbits around the center of the scene in a flat horizontal circle.

Use delta time so the orbit speed is smooth on fast and slow computers.

## Done when

- [ ] `cargo run` shows lit models with visible shading
- [ ] The light source is visible as a small marker
- [ ] The light orbits smoothly without judder
- [ ] Motion uses delta time, not frame count
- [ ] Lighting includes ambient, diffuse, and specular parts
- [ ] The light marker uses a separate render pipeline with its own shaders
- [ ] The light marker is not forced into the main lit-object pipeline

## Depends on

Finish #9 first.

## Time estimate

Local estimate: **6–10 hours** of focused work.

Assumes basic Rust knowledge, no prior graphics experience, and the type-along + small-variation working pattern. This is a local estimate for this issue only; see `README.md` for the global cursus estimate.
issues.title: ch10: Working with Lights

issues.body:
## Goal, in plain English

Make model surfaces look like they have tiny bumps and details, even when the mesh is still simple.

This is called normal mapping.

Tutorial: https://sotrh.github.io/learn-wgpu/intermediate/tutorial11-normals/

## Important project rule

Build this in the main app using shared `src/` code. Do not make a totally separate implementation.

## What you are learning

- Normal = a direction pointing away from a surface. Lighting uses it.
- Normal map = a texture that stores fake surface directions.
- Tangent space = a local coordinate system on the surface of the model.
- Per-fragment = done for each pixel.
- Flat-normal lighting = lighting that does not use a normal map.
- Uniform = small value sent to the shader.
- Specialization/toggle value = a cheap way to tell the shader which mode to use.
- Swapping pipelines = changing the whole GPU recipe. It works, but is heavier than a simple uniform toggle.

## What to build

1. Follow Learn Wgpu chapter 11.
2. Load normal-map textures.
3. Use tangent-space normal mapping in the fragment shader.
4. Make the model show richer surface detail.

## Extra beginner-friendly variation

Add a key toggle, for example `N`.

- Normal mapping on = bumpy/detail look.
- Normal mapping off = flatter look.

This lets you compare the same model both ways and actually see what normal mapping does.

## Done when

- [ ] `cargo run` shows a model with normal mapping enabled by default
- [ ] Pressing the toggle key switches normal mapping on/off
- [ ] The difference is obvious: surface bumps/details appear and disappear
- [ ] The toggle uses a uniform or similar cheap shader value
- [ ] The toggle does not swap whole render pipelines

## Depends on

Finish #10 first.

## Time estimate

Local estimate: **5–8 hours** of focused work.

Assumes basic Rust knowledge, no prior graphics experience, and the type-along + small-variation working pattern. This is a local estimate for this issue only; see `README.md` for the global cursus estimate.
issues.title: ch11: Normal Mapping

issues.body:
## Goal, in plain English

Make the camera controls feel like a real 3D camera.

Tutorial: https://sotrh.github.io/learn-wgpu/intermediate/tutorial12-camera/

## Important project rule

Build this in the main app using shared `src/` code. Do not make a totally separate implementation.

## What you are learning

- `CameraController` = code that owns camera input and movement rules.
- Mouse-look = moving the mouse rotates the camera view.
- View matrix = camera position/direction.
- Projection matrix = 3D-to-screen settings.
- Decoupled = split into separate pieces instead of one blob.
- Raw mouse deltas = how far the mouse moved since the last event.
- OS pointer acceleration = the operating system changing mouse movement speed. Raw deltas avoid this.
- Delta-time scaled = movement uses seconds, not frames, so speed is stable.

## What to build

1. Follow Learn Wgpu chapter 12.
2. Refactor camera input/state into a `CameraController`.
3. Add smooth WASD movement.
4. Add mouse-look.
5. Keep view and projection logic cleanly separated.
6. Use raw mouse movement from `DeviceEvent::MouseMotion`.
7. Make movement speed use delta time.

## Extra beginner-friendly variation

Add a freeze camera key, for example `F`.

- Press `F`: camera stops responding to input.
- Press `F` again: camera starts responding again.
- Rendering continues while frozen.

This is useful when you want to inspect the scene without accidentally moving.

## Done when

- [ ] `cargo run` has smooth WASD movement and mouse-look
- [ ] Pressing the freeze key stops camera input
- [ ] Pressing the freeze key again resumes camera input
- [ ] Rendering continues at full speed while the camera is frozen
- [ ] There is a visible frozen indicator, such as window title text, on-screen text, or a console print
- [ ] Mouse-look uses `DeviceEvent::MouseMotion`, not cursor position from `WindowEvent`
- [ ] Movement is in units/second using delta time, not units/frame

## Depends on

Finish #11 first.

## Time estimate

Local estimate: **5–8 hours** of focused work.

Assumes basic Rust knowledge, no prior graphics experience, and the type-along + small-variation working pattern. This is a local estimate for this issue only; see `README.md` for the global cursus estimate.
issues.title: ch12: A Better Camera

issues.body:
## Goal, in plain English

Render the scene in HDR, then convert it back to normal screen colors.

HDR lets the renderer store very bright values without immediately crushing them. Tone mapping turns those values into colors your monitor can show.

Tutorial: https://sotrh.github.io/learn-wgpu/intermediate/tutorial13-hdr/

This is the final Phase 1 chapter.

## Important project rule

Build this in the main app using shared `src/` code. Do not make a totally separate implementation.

## What you are learning

- HDR = High Dynamic Range. It can store a wider range of brightness.
- Float texture = texture that stores floating-point color values, useful for HDR.
- Tone mapping = converting HDR colors into normal display colors.
- Swap chain = the final images shown in the window.
- Fullscreen pass = drawing one full-screen triangle/quad to process the final image.
- Gamma correction = adjusts colors so brightness looks right on the screen.
- Exposure = brightness control, like camera exposure.
- Uniform = small value sent to the shader.

## What to build

1. Follow Learn Wgpu chapter 13.
2. Render the scene into an HDR float texture.
3. Add a second fullscreen pass.
4. In that pass, tone-map the HDR texture into the final swap-chain image.
5. Apply gamma correction.

## Extra beginner-friendly variation

Add runtime exposure controls.

For example:

- `+` increases exposure
- `-` decreases exposure

Show the current exposure value in the window title.

The point is to see how HDR and tone mapping respond when the scene gets brighter or darker.

## Done when

- [ ] `cargo run` renders through an HDR pass
- [ ] The HDR result is tone-mapped to the swap chain
- [ ] Exposure keys visibly change scene brightness
- [ ] Changing exposure does not break colors
- [ ] The current exposure value is displayed, window title is fine
- [ ] Write at least one `IDEAS.md` note about Phase 1: what surprised you, and what you would reuse for Pong

## Depends on

Finish #12 first.

## Time estimate

Local estimate: **6–10 hours** of focused work.

Assumes basic Rust knowledge, no prior graphics experience, and the type-along + small-variation working pattern. This is a local estimate for this issue only; see `README.md` for the global cursus estimate.
issues.title: ch13: HDR Rendering

issues.body:
## Goal, in plain English

Build a complete 2D Pong game from the Learn Wgpu showcase tutorial.

This is the first full game in the project: paddles, ball, scoring, winning, and a reset loop.

Tutorial: https://sotrh.github.io/learn-wgpu/showcase/pong/

## Important project rule

Build this in the main app using shared `src/` code. Do not make a totally separate implementation.

This chapter may be big enough to need several shared modules in `src/`. Decide on purpose. Keep the code easy to follow.

## Why this matters

This tutorial is the main Learn Wgpu example where rendering, input, game state, and the game loop all work together.

You will use it as a working reference before building 3D Pong in Phase 2b.

## What you are learning

- Renderer = code that draws the game.
- Input = keyboard/player controls.
- Game state = data like ball position, paddle position, score, and current mode.
- Game loop = update the game, then draw it, over and over.
- State machine = clear game modes, such as `Serving`, `Playing`, and `GameOver`.
- `wgpu_glyph` or similar = a crate that can draw text on the screen.
- AI paddle = computer-controlled paddle.
- `WIN_SCORE` = constant for how many points are needed to win.

## What to build

1. Follow the 2D Pong showcase tutorial.
2. Build paddles, ball, scoring, and win condition.
3. Render the score as on-screen text.
4. Use a simple state machine with at least:
   - `Serving`
   - `Playing`
   - `GameOver`
5. Reset the game after someone wins.

## Extra beginner-friendly variations

1. Make AI difficulty configurable.
   - Put a constant near the top of the file/module.

## Goal, in plain English

Add the Pong ball and make it bounce in 3D.

Still no scoring yet. For now the ball just bounces forever.

## Important project rule

Build this in the main app using shared `src/` code. Do not make a totally separate implementation.

## What you are learning

- Entity = a thing in the game world, like the ball or a paddle.
- `vec3` = 3 numbers together: x, y, and z.
- Position = where something is.
- Velocity = how fast something moves and in what direction.
- Constant velocity = speed/direction stay the same until a bounce changes them.
- Delta time = seconds since the last frame. Use it so motion is smooth at different FPS.
- Collision = when two things touch or overlap.
- Reflect = flip a movement direction after a bounce.
- Bounding box = simple box used to test if things overlap.
- Rendering = drawing. Collision math should be separate from drawing code.

## What to build

1. Add a ball with:
   - position as `vec3`
   - velocity as `vec3`
2. Move the ball using delta time.
3. No gravity.
4. No drag/friction.
5. Bounce off all 4 court walls.
6. Bounce off both paddles when the ball hits a paddle bounding box.
7. Do not add scoring yet.
8. If the ball reaches the back wall, just bounce it for now. Scoring comes in #17.

## Simple collision idea

When the ball hits a side wall, flip the matching velocity part:

- hits left/right wall: flip x velocity
- hits top/bottom wall: flip y velocity
- hits paddle: flip z velocity

## Done when

- [ ] `cargo run` shows a ball bouncing inside the court
- [ ] Ball motion is smooth and frame-rate independent
- [ ] Ball reflects correctly off all 4 walls
- [ ] Ball reflects correctly off both paddles
- [ ] Collision math lives in a function/module separate from rendering

## Goal, in plain English

Turn 3D Pong into a real playable game.

The player controls one paddle. The computer controls the other. The game tracks score and can end.

## Important project rule

Build this in the main app using shared `src/` code. Do not make a totally separate implementation.

## What you are learning

- Player paddle = the paddle controlled by you.
- AI paddle = the paddle controlled by the computer.
- AI = simple computer behavior. It does not need to be smart.
- Clamped = not allowed to move outside the court bounds.
- Lag = the AI follows slowly instead of instantly.
- z-plane = a flat slice at one z position, like the paddle's end of the court.
- Scoring = giving a point when someone misses the ball.
- Opposing player = the other side.
- Win condition = rule that decides when the game is over.
- `WIN_SCORE` = constant for points needed to win.
- Reset = put the game back at the start.

## What to build

1. Add keyboard controls for the player paddle.
   - WASD or arrow keys are fine.
   - Move in x/y.
   - Clamp movement so the paddle stays inside the court opening.
2. Add AI for the other paddle.
   - It follows the ball's x/y position.
   - Give it capped speed or lag so it is beatable.
   - No prediction needed.
3. Add scoring.
   - If the ball passes a paddle without being hit, the other player scores.
   - Reset the ball to the center after a score.
   - Randomize the new ball direction a little.
4. Add a win condition.
   - First to `WIN_SCORE` wins.
   - Show the winner in the window title or console.
   - Press a key to reset scores and start a new game.

## Done when

- [ ] `cargo run` is a playable 3D Pong game
- [ ] Player paddle responds to keyboard input
- [ ] Player paddle stays inside court bounds
- [ ] AI can score
- [ ] Player can score
- [ ] AI is beatable but not useless
- [ ] Scoring works correctly
- [ ] Ball reset works correctly after scoring
- [ ] Win condition shows a visible win state
- [ ] Pressing a key resets after a win

issues.body:
## Goal, in plain English

Make it easy to tell how deep into the court the ball is.

In 3D Pong, players can lose because they cannot judge the ball's z position. This issue adds a visual helper so the ball's depth is obvious.

## Important project rule

Build this in the main app using shared `src/` code. Do not make a totally separate implementation.

## What you are learning

- Depth perception = your ability to tell how far away something is.
- z position = how far forward/back the ball is in the court.
- Visual cue = extra visual help for the player's eyes.
- Ground-plane shadow = a flat dark circle on the floor under the ball.
- Grid texture = grid lines on the floor that make distance easier to read.
- Projected indicator line = a line from the ball straight down to the floor.
- Perspective foreshortening = far things look smaller/closer together, which helps the brain read depth.
- Semi-transparent = partly see-through.

## Pick one visual cue

Choose one of these:

### Option A: ground-plane shadow

Draw a flat, semi-transparent dark disc on the court floor directly under the ball. Move it every frame as the ball moves.

This is the recommended first try because it usually looks clean.

### Option B: grid-textured court floor

Put a regular grid on the floor. The grid lines help the eye understand distance.

### Option C: projected indicator line

Draw a thin line from the ball straight down to the floor.

## Human eyeball check

You cannot fully know which cue feels best until you try it in motion.

Try Option A first. If it does not feel clear, switch to B or C.

Write an `IDEAS.md` note explaining:

- what you tried
- what you picked
- why it worked best

## Done when

- [ ] `cargo run` includes a clear depth cue
- [ ] The ball's z position is easy to understand while playing
- [ ] You can play a full game without losing because you misjudged depth
- [ ] `IDEAS.md` explains which cue you picked, what you tried, and why

## Depends on

Finish #17 first.

## Time estimate

Local estimate: **4–8 hours** of focused work.

Assumes basic Rust knowledge, no prior graphics experience, and the type-along + small-variation working pattern. This is a local estimate for this issue only; see `README.md` for the global cursus estimate.

## Goal, in plain English

Make 3D Pong feel better, then write down what you learned.

This is the final issue of Phase 2 and the v1 milestone.

## Important project rule

Build this in the main app using shared `src/` code. Do not make a totally separate implementation.

## What you are learning

- Polish = small improvements that make the game feel better.
- Tuning = adjusting numbers until the game feels right.
- Ball speed = how fast the ball moves.
- Paddle responsiveness = how quickly the paddle reacts to input.
- Camera angle = where the camera sits and points.
- FOV = field of view; how wide the camera sees.
- AI difficulty = how hard the computer paddle is to beat.
- Jank = anything that looks or feels rough.
- Z-fighting = flickering caused when two surfaces are in almost the same place.
- Clipping = geometry cutting through other geometry or the camera.
- Motion stutter = uneven movement.
- Retrospective = a written note about what went well, what hurt, and what you would do differently.
- Coupling = when parts of the code depend on each other too much, making changes painful.

## What to tune

Play the game and adjust these until it feels reasonable:

- ball speed
- whether the ball speeds up a little after paddle hits
- paddle movement speed
- paddle input feel
- camera angle
- camera FOV
- AI speed/lag
- any visual glitches

## What to write in `IDEAS.md`

Write at least 200 words about the architecture.

Use simple questions:

- What parts of the code were easy to change?
- What parts were annoying to change?
- Which systems were too tightly connected?
- What would you do differently if starting over?
- Did building the "wrong" architecture teach you anything useful?
- Would you build a bigger game next, or clean up the engine first?

This note is for future you. It does not need to sound fancy.

## Done when

- [ ] 3D Pong is playable and feels reasonably tuned
- [ ] No obvious visual glitches happen during normal play
- [ ] `IDEAS.md` has a retrospective entry of at least 200 words
- [ ] `README.md` says project v1 is done
- [ ] `README.md` includes a short "what's next" note
